title: LinkedList
html:
Linked-list problems are pointer puzzles: almost every classic one is solved by two pointers moving at different speeds or distances, by reversing links in place, or by re-wiring nodes without allocating. This topic collects the problems interviewers actually ask and the handful of techniques that solve them.

Singly linked list — a chain of nodes where each node stores a value (data) and a reference to the next node (next); the last node's next is null. Only the head is kept — every other node is reached by following links, so random access is O(n) but splicing nodes in and out is O(1) once you stand next to them.

Recap: what costs what

OperationSingly linked listDynamic array
Access i-th elementO(n) — walk from headO(1)
Insert / delete at headO(1)O(n) — shift everything
Insert / delete after a known nodeO(1) — re-wire two linksO(n)
Insert / delete at tailO(n) (O(1) with a tail pointer)amortised O(1)
SearchO(n)O(n) (O(log n) if sorted)
Memory per elementvalue + one pointer, scatteredvalue only, contiguous and cache-friendly

The problems in this topic exploit the one thing a list does better than an array: moving a node costs O(1) and no allocation. Reversing, merging, swapping pairs and segregating are all done by changing next pointers, never by copying values into a new container.

The techniques behind every problem

Slow and fast pointers

slow moves one node per step, fast two. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle; if fast ever catches slow, there is a loop. Used for: middle, palindrome, loop detection.

Two pointers a fixed gap apart

Send first ahead by n nodes, then move both together; when first falls off, second is n from the end. Used for: nth node from end, intersection (after aligning lengths).

Reverse links in place

Three pointers prev, curr, next flip each link in one pass. Used for: reverse, reverse in groups of k, palindrome (reverse the second half).

Dummy head node

A throwaway node in front of the list removes every “is this the first node?” special case. Used for: merge, pairwise swap, deleting nodes.

Hash the node references

A set or map keyed by node identity (not value) gives a straightforward O(n)-space solution — the baseline you beat with pointer tricks. Used for: loop, intersection, clone.

Re-wire instead of allocate

Thread existing nodes into new sublists (even/odd, merged) or interleave copies inside the original list (clone). Used for: segregate, clone with random pointers.

Node and helpers used in every solution

Every program below carries the same three pieces: a Node, build(values) that turns an array into a list, and toStr(head) that prints a list as space-separated values. They are the only boilerplate — the solutions themselves are the functions in between.

Key point

build prepends from the back of the array so the list comes out in array order without a tail pointer. In C++ the nodes are allocated with new and never freed in these short programs — fine for a demo, a leak in real code; a destructor or unique_ptr chain fixes that.

Middle of a linked list

Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: 30
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40
Output: 30 (the second of the two middle nodes)

Idea

Two pointers start at the head. slow advances one node, fast two. When fast runs off the end, fast has covered the whole list and slow exactly half of it — slow is standing on the middle. One pass, no counting.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

For an even length this returns the second middle (30 of 10 20 30 40). To get the first middle instead, loop while fast.next and fast.next.next — that variant is exactly what the palindrome check below uses, because it wants slow at the end of the first half.

Nth node from the end

Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, n = 2
Output: 40
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, n = 6
Output: none (list is shorter than n)

Idea

Move first ahead by n nodes. Now move first and second together; the gap between them stays n, so when first falls off the end, second is exactly n nodes from the end. The naive alternative — count the length, then walk len − n nodes — also works in O(n) but needs two passes.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Check first for null inside the first loop. Without that check, n larger than the length dereferences null — a crash in C++/Java/JavaScript and an AttributeError in Python. “Delete the nth node from the end” is the same walk with a dummy head so that deleting the first node is not a special case.

Reverse a linked list

Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: 50 → 40 → 30 → 20 → 10

Idea

Iterative: walk the list once with three pointers. prev is the already-reversed part, curr is the node being flipped, next saves the rest so it is not lost when curr.next is overwritten. Recursive: reverse everything after head, then make the old second node (head.next) point back to head and set head.next = null — head becomes the tail.

Time O(n)Space O(1) iterative · O(n) recursive (call stack)
Pitfall

Forgetting to save next before curr.next = prev loses the rest of the list. In the recursive version, forgetting head.next = null leaves a cycle between the last two nodes — the first node still points at the second, which now points back. Prefer the iterative version in production: the recursive one uses one stack frame per node and overflows on long lists (Python at ~1000).

Reverse a linked list in groups of k

Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50 → 60, k = 3
Output: 30 → 20 → 10 → 60 → 50 → 40
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, k = 3
Output: 30 → 20 → 10 → 50 → 40

Idea

Reverse the first k nodes with the ordinary three-pointer loop. The group's old first node (head) is now its last node, so its next must point at the result of reversing the rest — either a recursive call, or the next group in an iterative loop. The last group is reversed even when it holds fewer than k nodes (the LeetCode variant leaves a short tail untouched — add a length check if that is required).

Recursive — the natural way to express “reverse this group, then link to the reversed rest”:

Time O(n)Space O(n / k) recursion depth

Iterative — same work, constant extra space. Remember the first node of each group: after the group is reversed it is the group's tail, and the previous group's tail must be pointed at the new head of this group.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The two bugs here are both linking bugs: forgetting head.next = … after the recursive call (groups come back disconnected), or linking prev_tail to the group's first node instead of its new head prev.

Detect a loop — hash set of visited nodes

Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, and 50 → 30
Output: Yes
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: No

Idea

Walk the list, putting each node's reference (not its value — values may repeat) into a set. The first node already in the set is the loop entry; reaching null means no loop. Simple and O(n) time, but O(n) extra memory — the baseline Floyd's algorithm improves on.

Key point

The set must hold references: in C++ an unordered_set<Node*> keyed by address, in Java a HashSet<Node> (identity semantics because Node does not override equals/hashCode), in JavaScript a Set of objects. A set of values would report a false loop on 1 → 2 → 1.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Key point

Two other O(1)-space tricks you may see: a visited flag inside each node (needs a field you usually cannot add), or pointing every visited node's next at a sentinel dummy node (destroys the list). Floyd's algorithm needs neither.

Detect a loop — Floyd's cycle detection

Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50, and 50 → 30
Output: Yes
Input: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
Output: No

Idea

Run slow (one step) and fast (two steps) from the head. If there is no loop, fast reaches null. If there is a loop, both pointers eventually circle inside it, and fast gains exactly one node on slow every step — so it must land on slow within one lap. Two pointers, no memory.

1
Initialise
slow = head, fast = head.
2
Advance
Each step: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next. Stop with “no loop” when fast or fast.next is null.
3
Compare
If slow is the same node as fast, there is a loop.

Why they must meet. fast enters the loop no later than slow. Suppose that when slow enters the loop, fast is k nodes ahead of it (0 ≤ k < n for a loop of length n) — equivalently, fast is n − k nodes behind slow going round the circle. Every step slow moves one and fast moves two, so the gap behind closes by exactly one node per step. After n − k steps the gap is zero: they stand on the same node. Because the gap shrinks by one (not two), fast can never jump over slow.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Compare the nodes, not their values (slow is fast / == on references) — a list with repeated values has no loop. And test fast.next as well as fast before stepping twice; fast.next.next on the last node is a null dereference.

Detect and remove a loop

Example

Input: 10 → 15 → 5 → 20, and 20 → 15
Output: 10 → 15 → 5 → 20 (loop of length 3 starting at 15 removed)

Idea

Floyd's meeting point is not the loop's first node — but it is a fixed distance from it. Move slow back to head, keep fast at the meeting point, and advance both one step at a time: they meet exactly at the first node of the loop. Then walk round the loop once more to find the node whose next is that first node, and set its next to null.

1
Detect
Run Floyd's algorithm. If slow and fast never meet, there is no loop — stop.
2
Loop length (variation 1)
From the meeting point, walk round until you are back: the number of steps is the loop length n.
3
First node of the loop (variation 2)
Put slow at head, leave fast at the meeting point. Move both one step until they are equal — that node is the loop start.
4
Cut
From the loop start, walk until node.next is the loop start again; that node is the last node of the loop. Set its next = null.

Why moving one pointer back to the head works. Let m be the distance from head to the loop start, n the loop length, and k the distance from the loop start to the meeting point. When they meet, slow has walked m + k + x·n and fast twice that, m + k + y·n, for some lap counts x, y:

2(m + k + x·n) = m + k + y·n ⟹ m + k = (y − 2x)·n

So m + k is a multiple of the loop length. A pointer that starts at the meeting point (already k into the loop) and walks m more steps is m + k ≡ 0 (mod n) into the loop — i.e. back at the loop start. A pointer that starts at head and walks m steps is also at the loop start. Walking both at the same speed, they coincide for the first time exactly there.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

When the loop starts at the head itself (m = 0), the meeting point is the loop start, so the phase-2 loop runs zero times — no special case needed. The original notes handled that separately; the version above does not have to because it compares slow and fast directly rather than slow.next and fast.next.

Intersection point of two linked lists

Example

Input: A: 5 → 8 → 7 → 10 → 12 → 15, B: 9 → 10 → 12 → 15 (B's second node is A's node 10)
Output: 10

Baseline — hash set of nodes. Put every node of A in a set, then walk B and return the first node already present. O(m + n) time, O(m) space.

Efficient — align the lengths. Both lists share their whole tail from the intersection on, so they differ only in the number of nodes before it. Count both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then walk both together; the first time the two pointers are the same node is the intersection (or both reach null).

Idea

After skipping |len(A) − len(B)| nodes of the longer list, both pointers are the same distance from the end. From then on they move in lock-step, so they reach the shared tail at the same moment.

Time O(m + n)Space O(1)
Key point

No-counting variant: walk pa over A then B, and pb over B then A. Both travel exactly len(A) + len(B) nodes, so they reach the intersection together — or both hit null after the second list. Same complexity, slightly less code, harder to explain in an interview.

Pitfall

Intersection means the same node object, not equal values — 1 → 2 → 3 and 9 → 3 with two different 3 nodes do not intersect. Compare references.

Segregate even and odd nodes

Example

Input: 17 → 15 → 8 → 12 → 5
Output: 8 → 12 → 17 → 15 → 5 (all even values first, relative order preserved)

Naive — move odd nodes to the end. Find the last node, then traverse once more: every odd node is detached and appended after the current last node. Stop after processing the original last node, otherwise the nodes you just appended are visited again and the loop never ends.

One traversal — build two sublists and join them. Keep the start and end of an even sublist and of an odd sublist. Every node is appended to the end of its own sublist as it is visited, so each sublist keeps the original relative order. At the end, link the even tail to the odd head and terminate the odd tail.

Idea

Nothing is allocated and no node is moved twice: the four pointers even_start, even_end, odd_start, odd_end just thread the existing nodes into two chains, which are joined once.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

odd_end.next = None is the line everyone forgets. If the last node of the input is even, the odd tail still points at some even node that is now earlier in the list — and the result has a cycle that to_str would loop on forever. The same two-chain pattern solves “partition a list around a value x” and “odd/even positions” (LeetCode 328).

Pairwise swap nodes

Example

Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
Output: 2 → 1 → 4 → 3
Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
Output: 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5 (odd one out stays)

Swap the data. Walk two nodes at a time and exchange the values of each pair. Trivial — but it only works when swapping values is allowed and cheap. If nodes carry large payloads, or other code holds references to specific nodes (an LRU cache, an iterator), the values must stay with their nodes and the links have to be swapped instead.

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Swap the links. For each pair a → b, make the node before the pair point at b, b point at a, and a point at whatever followed b. A dummy node in front of the head removes the special case for the first pair (whose “node before” would otherwise not exist), and the new head is simply dummy.next.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Pairwise swap is “reverse in groups of k” with k = 2 and a short tail left alone. The dummy-head trick is worth memorising: it turns every “what if it is the first node?” branch into ordinary code.

Clone a linked list with random pointers

Example

Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 with random links 1→3, 2→1, 3→4, 4→2
Output: an independent copy with the same next and random structure

Each node has a second pointer, random, to any node in the list (or null). A plain copy that walks next cannot set random on the copies because the target copy may not exist yet — and even when it does, you have to find it. Two solutions: a map from original to copy, or a trick that stores the mapping inside the list itself.

Method 1 — dictionary from original to copy. Pass 1 creates a copy of every node and records copy_of[original] = copy. Pass 2 sets copy_of[node].next = copy_of[node.next] and copy_of[node].random = copy_of[node.random]; mapping null → null makes the end of the list and missing randoms fall out for free.

Time O(n)Space O(n) for the map

Method 2 — interleave the copies, O(1) extra space. Store the mapping in the list: insert each copy right after its original, so original.next is always its copy. Then copy.random = original.random.next finds the right copy in O(1) without a map. Finally unweave the two lists.

1
Interleave
For every original node o, create o' and insert it after o: 1 → 1' → 2 → 2' → 3 → 3' → 4 → 4'.
2
Set randoms
For every original o (step two at a time): o.next.random = o.random.next — the copy of o.random is the node right after it. Skip when o.random is null.
3
Unweave
Restore o.next = o.next.next and set o'.next = o'.next.next, splitting the chain back into the original list and the clone.
Time O(n)Space O(1) extra (the clone itself is O(n))
Pitfall

The original notes wrote curr.next.random = curr.random.next without checking curr.random — a null random crashes it. Also, step 3 must restore the originals' next pointers; a clone routine that leaves the input list interleaved has corrupted its caller's data.

Merge two sorted linked lists

Example

Input: 10 → 20 → 30 and 5 → 25
Output: 5 → 10 → 20 → 25 → 30

Idea

Exactly the merge step of merge sort, but without a temporary array: compare the two heads, append the smaller to the result's tail, advance that list. When one list is exhausted, the whole remainder of the other is already sorted — link it in one step. A dummy head means the result's tail always exists, so no first-node special case.

Time O(m + n)Space O(1)

The same idea reads naturally as recursion — the head of the merged list is the smaller head, and its next is the merge of what remains. Elegant, but it uses one stack frame per node, so keep it for short lists:

Key point

Merge is the building block of merge sort on a linked list — the sorting algorithm of choice for lists, because splitting (find the middle with slow/fast) and merging need no random access and no extra array: O(n log n) time, O(log n) stack. Merging k sorted lists uses a min-heap of the k current heads.

Palindrome linked list

Example

Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 2 → 1
Output: Yes
Input: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
Output: No
Input: R → A → D → A → R
Output: Yes

Naive — copy the values onto a stack. Push every value, then walk the list again popping: pops come out in reverse order, so each pop must equal the current node. O(n) time but O(n) extra space.

Efficient — reverse the second half in place. Find the end of the first half with slow/fast, reverse the second half, and walk the two halves together comparing values. Then reverse the second half again to restore the list — callers do not expect a read-only query to scramble their data.

Idea

A palindrome reads the same backwards. Reversing just the second half turns “compare position i with position n − 1 − i” into a plain forward walk over two lists of (almost) equal length — no index arithmetic, no extra memory.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Use the fast.next and fast.next.next loop condition so that slow lands on the end of the first half (the middle node for odd length). With the plain fast and fast.next condition from the middle-finding problem, slow would be one node too far and the halves misaligned. Returning early on a mismatch without restoring the list is the other classic slip — the version above breaks out, restores, then returns.

Interview Q&A

Why does Floyd's algorithm use speeds 1 and 2 — would 1 and 3 work?

Any two different speeds work for detection: once both pointers are in a loop of length n, the gap changes by a constant each step and eventually hits a multiple of n. Speeds 1 and 2 are chosen because the gap shrinks by exactly one per step (guaranteeing a meeting within n steps of entering the loop) and because the m + k = multiple of n identity makes finding the loop start a one-liner. With speed 3 the second phase no longer works unchanged.

How do you find the start of the loop after detecting it, and why does it work?

Keep one pointer at the meeting point and move the other back to the head; advance both one step at a time — they meet at the loop's first node. Proof: with m = head-to-loop-start, k = loop-start-to-meeting-point and n = loop length, fast has travelled twice as far as slow, which gives m + k = (y − 2x)·n, a multiple of n. So after m steps the pointer from the meeting point has gone m + k ≡ 0 (mod n) into the loop — it is at the loop start, exactly where the pointer from the head has also arrived.

How would you detect a loop or find an intersection without Floyd's algorithm?

Hash the node references: a set of visited nodes finds a loop (first repeat) or an intersection (first node of B already seen while walking A) in O(n) time and O(n) space. It is the baseline — mention it first, then improve to O(1) space with slow/fast pointers or length alignment.

Reverse a linked list in O(1) space — iterative or recursive?

Iterative: three pointers (prev, curr, next) in one pass, O(1) extra space. The recursive version is shorter to write but uses O(n) stack — one frame per node — and overflows on long lists. Interviewers usually want the iterative version and then ask for the recursive one as a follow-up (or vice versa).

What is the dummy-head trick and when do you use it?

Create a throwaway node whose next is the real head, and work from it. Every operation that might change the head (insert at front, delete the first node, merge, pairwise swap) then has no special case — the first real node is just “the node after dummy”. Return dummy.next at the end. It costs one allocation and saves a branch and a bug.

Clone a list with random pointers in O(1) extra space — how?

Interleave: insert each node's copy right after it (1 → 1' → 2 → 2' …), so the copy of any node x is x.next. Set x.next.random = x.random.next for every original, then unweave the two lists in one more pass. Three passes, O(n) time, no map. The hash-map version is the simpler O(n)-space baseline.

Which sorting algorithm fits a linked list best, and why not quicksort?

Merge sort: split with slow/fast pointers, merge by re-linking nodes — O(n log n) with no random access and no extra array. Quicksort and heapsort need O(1) index access to partition or sift; on a list every arr[i] becomes an O(n) walk.
